parent.name: Philidor Defense: Exchange Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4
parent.overview: After 3.d4 exd4 White recaptures (4.Nxd4 is the main line; Morphy's 4.Qxd4 is the alternative) and then has a space advantage and the more comfortable game. Black replies ...Nf6 and ...Be7, castles quickly and aims for a compact position (often with ...Nbd7 or ...c5/...c6 later) with king safety first, using ...d5 or ...c5 as freeing breaks. The structure is passive but not refuted: White cannot force a tactical win, but must prove an edge. Sources call it a sound, practical defence, an easy entry point for club players that is rarely used by top players because it concedes space; Aronian is mentioned as an occasional user. The Antoshin set-up (6.Be2) is a common White try.

root.name: Van Geet Opening: Kluever Gambit
root.moves: 1. Nc3 f5 2. e4 fxe4 3. d3

parent.name: Van Geet Opening
parent.overview: White develops a knight to c3, controlling e4 and d5, and keeps the pawn structure undecided to choose a set-up once Black replies. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Queen's Gambit and English structures are not available without reorganising. Main replies: 1...d5 (the cleanest; 2.e4 transposes to obscure Scandinavian lines, or the Van Geet Attack after 2...d4 3.Nce2), 1...e5 (then 2.e4 Vienna Game, the most common transposition in the database, or 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Napoleon Attack), 1...Nf6 (one of the most unpleasant replies for White) and 1...c5 (transposing to Closed Sicilian or inferior-placed-knight lines). Sources call it sound and low-theory but unambitious: Black equalises with accurate play, so it earns points from surprise rather than from an edge, and masters play it under 1% of the time, though some strong correspondence players use it. The database root has few games itself; most of the subtree (about 290M games) is Vienna, Closed Sicilian and Chigorin-style transpositions that play like those openings.

root.name: Ponziani Opening: Caro Gambit
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. c3 d5 4. Qa4 Bd7

parent.name: Pirc Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...d6 and, after 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3, ...g6 and ...Bg7, letting White build the broad e4-d4 centre and then undermining it from the flanks with ...c5 or ...e5 (hypermodern: the bigger White's centre, the bigger the target). The root is a crossroads: 1...d6 can transpose to the Philidor (3...e5 or ...c6) or to the Modern. White's replies run from sharp (Austrian Attack 4.f4, 150 Attack 4.Be3 with Qd2, Bh6 and h4-h5, Byrne 4.Bg5, Bayonet h4) to unhurried (Classical 4.Nf3 with Be2 and castling, fianchetto). Typical play is imbalanced: White gets space and often a kingside attack, Black gets a solid fianchettoed king and counterplay on the queenside and with central breaks. It is sound but has a reputation for giving White chances; Kasparov doubted it for the top level (s1), though Caruana, Anand and Grischuk have used it (s2).

root.name: Petrov's Defense: Kaufmann Attack
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4 5. c4

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Modern Defense
parent.overview: Against 1.d4 Black plays 1...g6, fianchettoing the king's bishop (...Bg7) and delaying the knight on f6 and any central commitment. The idea is hypermodern: let White build a pawn centre, then attack it from the flanks with ...d6 and ...c5 or ...e5, with queenside play (...b5, ...a5) backed by the Bg7. Because ...Nf6 is delayed it can still become a King's Indian (after c4 and Nc3), a Pirc (after e4) or a Grünfeld, or stay a separate Modern. White's common set-ups are a classical centre (c4, e4, Nc3, Be3), the Averbakh with c4, or the pseudo-Austrian or Samisch-like f4/f3 centres with a kingside space attack. Sources disagree on the character: the line is balanced and sound but can become very sharp and awkward for Black if the kingside weakens.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 Nf6
parent.overview: Black counterattacks e4 at once with 3...Nf6. In the main line 4.O-O Nxe4 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5 Nf5 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8 (the Berlin Wall endgame) queens leave the board early, Black gives up castling and accepts doubled c-pawns, and in return gets the bishop pair and a very solid structure; White has a healthy kingside pawn majority and a small, long-term edge that is very hard to convert. Neither side has attacking chances; the game is a technical endgame where Black holds with accurate defence and White tries to squeeze. White can avoid it with 4.d3 (the Anti-Berlin), which keeps queens on and gives slow Italian-like manoeuvring with Black choosing ...Bc5 or ...d6. The line was revived by Kramnik as a drawing weapon against Kasparov in 2000 and is now a staple of elite play.
